1.question: [Geography] Which two départements make up Alsace?
1.explanation: Alsace consists of Bas-Rhin (Lower Rhine, north, capital Strasbourg) and Haut-Rhin (Upper Rhine, south, capital Colmar). "Bas" is in the north and "Haut" in the south, from the relative position along the Rhine rather than altitude.
2.question: [History] When did Alsace officially gain AOC status?
2.explanation: Alsace received a provisional decree in 1945, gained official AOC status in 1962, founded CIVA in 1963, received the dedicated Grand Cru decree in 1975, and VT / SGN were officially named in 1984.
3.question: [Climate] What is the main reason Colmar receives only about 500–600 mm of rain a year?
3.options.0: The direct influence of a Mediterranean climate
3.options.1: The Vosges block Atlantic westerlies, creating a marked rain shadow
3.options.2: Being in an inland basin, it is completely unaffected by maritime climate
3.options.3: A purely recent anomaly of climate change
3.explanation: The Vosges greatly weaken the moisture carried by prevailing Atlantic westerlies, creating a marked rain shadow that makes Alsace (especially around Colmar) one of France's driest regions, with annual rainfall comparable to Montpellier on the Mediterranean coast.
4.question: [Geology] Why are most Alsace vineyards located on complex, varied fault zones?
4.options.0: Because frequent earthquakes keep changing the soil
4.options.1: Fifty million years ago the Vosges and Black Forest collapsed together to form the Rhine plain, and rock layers of different ages were re-exposed along the fault edges
4.options.2: Because human clearing practices have mixed up the strata
4.options.3: It only happens at a few exceptional sites
4.explanation: Fifty million years ago the Vosges and Black Forest were one massif; in the Tertiary the crust collapsed to form the Rhine plain, so rock layers accumulated in different geological ages were re-exposed along the fault edges. Alsace's vineyards sit exactly there, so many villages have several different soil layers at once.
5.question: [Varieties] Which is Alsace's most planted variety?
5.explanation: Riesling covers 21.68% of Alsace's total vineyard area, the most planted variety, called "the king of Alsace wines"; Pinot Blanc (21.21%) follows close behind.
6.question: [Varieties] What other name did Alsace Pinot Gris once have, and when was it formally dropped?
6.options.1: "Tokay d'Alsace", formally dropped from the 2007 vintage
6.explanation: Pinot Gris was once called "Tokay d'Alsace" or "Tokay-Pinot Gris". Under an agreement reached in 1993 between Alsace, Hungary and the EU, the name Tokay was formally dropped from the 2007 vintage, because it easily suggested a link with Hungary's Tokaji sweet wines.
7.question: [Varieties] What is Alsace's only black grape variety, and what was it traditionally mainly made into?
7.options.0: Merlot, mainly made into red wine
7.options.1: Pinot Noir, traditionally made mostly into rosé
7.options.2: Cabernet Franc, mainly used for blends
7.explanation: Pinot Noir is the only black grape variety grown in Alsace and was traditionally made mostly into rosé, with good red only in very few exceptional vintages — although a "return to red" trend has emerged in recent years.
8.question: [AOC Classification] Roughly what share of Alsace's total output is Alsace Grand Cru?
8.explanation: Alsace Grand Cru makes up only about 4% of the region's output (2009 data: 48,295 hl, 4.13%), the rarest tier at the top of the pyramid; base Alsace AOC makes up about 74%.
9.question: [Label] If an Alsace label says "Pinot", which varieties might it represent?
9.options.0: It can only be Pinot Blanc
9.options.1: It can only be Pinot Noir
9.options.2: One of Auxerrois, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir (vinified as white) or Pinot Gris, or a blend of them
9.options.3: It can only be Pinot Gris
9.explanation: The "Pinot" or "Klevner" designation can stand for any one of the four varieties Auxerrois B, Pinot Blanc B, Pinot Noir N (vinified as white) and Pinot Gris G, or a blend of them — a detail of Alsace labelling rules that is easy to misunderstand.
10.question: [Grand Cru] Which two Grand Crus allow blending of several varieties?
10.explanation: Altenberg de Bergheim (Riesling 50–70% + Pinot Gris 10–25% + Gewurztraminer 10–25%) and Kaefferkopf (Gewurztraminer 60–80% + Riesling 10–40% + Pinot Gris up to 30%) are the only two Alsace Grand Crus that allow blending.
11.question: [VT / SGN] Which four varieties are the only ones allowed for VT and SGN sweet wine designations?
11.explanation: VT / SGN are limited to the four "noble" varieties Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Riesling and Muscat — also, in principle, the authorised varieties of Alsace Grand Cru (with the exceptions of Sylvaner at Zotzenberg and Pinot Noir at some Grand Crus), showing the consistent regulatory logic of Alsace for these four core varieties.
12.question: [Yield] What is the base yield limit for Alsace Grand Cru, and how much lower is it than the base Alsace tier (80 hl/ha)?
12.options.0: 90 hl/ha, slightly higher than the base tier
12.options.1: 55 hl/ha, about 70% of the base tier
12.options.2: 20 hl/ha, only a quarter of the base tier
12.options.3: The yield rules for the two are identical
12.explanation: The base yield limit for Alsace Grand Cru is only 55 hl/ha (PLC up to 66 hl/ha), clearly lower than the base Alsace tier's 80 hl/ha — low yields let the vine concentrate its resources on a limited number of bunches, raising concentration, in line with Grand Cru's top-quality requirement.
13.message: 🎉 Congratulations on completing the Level 1 final assessment! You have built a solid foundation in Alsace wine!
13.keyPoints.0: ✅ Geography: two départements, Bas-Rhin (north, Strasbourg) and Haut-Rhin (south, Colmar)
13.keyPoints.1: ✅ History: 1962 AOC, 1975 Grand Cru decree, 1984 VT/SGN named, 2007 the 51st Grand Cru (Kaefferkopf)
13.keyPoints.2: ✅ Climate and geology: Vosges rain shadow, temperature inversion, terroir diversity created by fault zones
13.keyPoints.3: ✅ Variety spectrum: Riesling (21.68%) leads, with Gewurztraminer / Pinot Gris / Muscat making up the four noble varieties
13.keyPoints.4: ✅ Three-tier AOC: Alsace → + denomination → Grand Cru; the more specific the name, the stricter the rules and the lower the yield
13.keyPoints.5: ✅ VT / SGN: limited to the four noble varieties, a sweet wine category with extremely strict thresholds
